extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, classical literature, and political/ethical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Plato's normative criteria for evaluating poetry, pleasures, souls, and regimes from Republic Books IX–X: guidance on mimesis, the hierarchy of pleasures/lives, justice as psychic harmony, and why tyranny is worst. Useful for analysing prescriptions about art, education, and moral psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of imitative poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “All poetical imitations are ruinous to the understanding of the hearers, and that the knowledge of their true nature is the only antidote to them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's rule: imitative (mimetic) poetry should not be received because it misleads the soul. He argues poets create mere appearances and therefore present untrue images that corrupt the hearer's understanding; the remedy is knowledge of the imitator's true nature and censoring such poetry in the ideal state. (Context: Book X introduction to imitation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis as appearance and untruth
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter (and by analogy the poet) is a 'creator of appearances' and thus produces that which is untrue — a copy twice removed from the Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato distinguishes the maker of forms (the craftsman or divine maker) from the artisan who copies appearances; painters create images of images. The implication for evaluation: works that merely imitate appearances are less true and therefore epistemically and morally inferior. This is used to justify exclusion of imitative arts from the ideal education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge lives by experience, wisdom, and reason (criterion of true pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience and wisdom and reason are the best judges of which life is most pleasant; pleasures approved by the lover of wisdom (reason) are the truest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato proposes that when assessing which life is most pleasant, the verdict of the one with the greatest experience of all pleasures and the faculty of reason (the philosopher) should be taken as authoritative. Thus intellectual pleasures outrank honor- or wealth-centered pleasures because the philosopher has experienced other pleasures and is equipped to judge by reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parts of the soul correspond to three pleasures/classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is divided into three principles: the rational (lover of wisdom), the spirited (lover of honour), and the appetitive (lover of gain); each has its own pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of character and life should map these soul-parts to social classes (philosophers, soldiers, money-makers). Each part's proper pleasure is judged truest when it follows reason; disorder (one part ruling another's domain) produces spurious pleasures and misery. Use this model to judge individual virtue and well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of lives by pleasantness: philosopher > soldier > money-maker
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the three classes, the lover of wisdom has the pleasantest life, next the lover of honour (soldier), and last the lover of gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the philosopher has the advantage of greater experience and the faculty of reason, his pleasures are purer and truer. This ordering is a practical evaluative rubric for ranking types of life and their attendant pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of constitutions by happiness and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five regimes: royal (best), timocratic, oligarchical, democratical, tyrannical (worst); the royal (just) is happiest, the tyrant most miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato uses the analogy between city and soul to order political regimes by virtue/pleasure. Evaluation of a regime should consider whether it approximates the rule of reason (royal) or descends toward disorder and appetite (tyranny). This ordering functions as a criterion for political assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny produces greatest misery
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyrannical soul and the tyrannical State are the most miserable: 'the tyrant is ... never allowed to go on a journey ... lives in his hole ... is beset with fear and is full of convulsions and distractions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato gives vivid examples (e.g., the master isolated from the city, forced to flatter slaves) to show tyranny's psychological and social effects: fear, insatiability, poverty of soul, loss of voluntary action. Use these characteristics as evaluative signs that a life/regime is tyrannical and miserable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as harmony: each part doing its own business
rubrics_metrics.description: When the whole soul follows the philosophical principle and there is no division, 'the several parts are just, and do each of them their own business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is evaluated as internal order/harmony of the soul (and by analogy, of the city). Practical guidance: cultivate the higher element (reason) so that appetitive and spirited parts perform their proper roles; assess individuals/polities by whether this harmony is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of law and education: cultivate the higher element
rubrics_metrics.description: The intention of the law is to be the ally of the whole city by establishing in children a principle analogous to the constitution of a state and cultivating the higher element (the guardian/ruler in the soul).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws, education, and institutions should aim to form the divine element within persons (reason) so citizens become friends and equals under a common order. Use this as a standard for evaluating legal/educational policy and cultural practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure pleasure is not merely cessation of pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Some pleasures (e.g., smell) have no antecedent pains; the notion that pleasure is only relief from pain is an appearance, not the reality of pure pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato distinguishes pleasures that are pure (no antecedent pain) from those that are reliefs of pain. When evaluating pleasures or the good life, prefer pleasures that partake more of invariable truth and essence (intellectual pleasures) over those that are transient bodily reliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice is ultimately unprofitable for the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: He who is undetected only gets worse, whereas he who is detected and punished may have the brutal part of his nature silenced and be humanized; thus injustice does not profit the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's moral-evaluative claim: even if injustice brings external gains undetected, it degrades the soul. Use this argument to evaluate ethical conduct, policy, or art that appears advantageous but promotes internal disorder; favour practices that perfect justice, temperance, and wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure pleasures by degree of 'real being' and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: That which partakes more of invariable, immortal, and true being (knowledge, virtue) yields more real and truer pleasure than what serves the body (food, drink).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metaphysical criterion ranks pleasures by their closeness to the Forms/true being: intellectual and virtuous pleasures count as higher quality. Use this when distinguishing authentic vs. illusory pleasures in moral evaluation.
